confidence_note: The old text's 1850 iPhone and 1950 transistor thought experiment is not tied to the book and is dropped. Confirmed: Johnson borrows adjacent possible from biologist Stuart Kauffman; he describes it as the set of ideas within reach from current knowledge and materials; his house-with-doors image, where opening a door shows new rooms; Charles Babbage's programmable computer idea of the 1830s as an example outside the adjacent possible, built about a century later; and the Leyden jar invented almost simultaneously by Von Kleist and Cunaeus. Exact details of Babbage's machine and who 'built' computers after are kept general.
facts: Johnson takes the term adjacent possible from the biologist Stuart Kauffman.
It means the ideas within reach given what is already known and available.
He pictures it as a house where each door you open shows new rooms and new doors.
So the boundaries of the adjacent possible grow as you explore them.
Charles Babbage conceived a programmable computer in the 1830s; with the knowledge and materials of the day it would have been entirely mechanical and very slow.
About a century later accumulated knowledge had expanded what was possible and computers were built on his basic blueprints.
In the mid-1700s Von Kleist and Cunaeus of Leyden developed the same electrical device, the Leyden jar, within about a year of each other.
tension: Babbage had the idea of a programmable computer a century before anyone could build one.
opening_idea: Start with Babbage in the 1830s and a machine nobody could build yet.

lessons.idea: Look at what is within one step of what exists today and start from there.
lessons.anchor: The adjacent possible as a house whose rooms expand as you open doors.

reflect_final: What tool, skill or contact you already have has a next step that you have not yet tried?

use_cases.situation: Your team wants a big leap.
use_cases.move: Ask what is one step away from what you already have, as in Johnson's house of doors.

use_cases.situation: A friend says their idea is too early.
use_cases.move: Ask which missing piece the idea is waiting for and whether anyone is building it.
List what you can already do and pick the next door that opens from it.

pocket_idea: Babbage's computer waited a century for its parts: ask which missing piece your idea waits for.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Babbage designed a programmable computer in the 1830s and had to wait about a century for the world to catch up.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Steven Johnson borrows adjacent possible from biologist Stuart Kauffman: the ideas within reach of what exists. Babbage imagined a programmable computer in the 1830s, but with the materials of his day it would have been mechanical and slow. A century later it was buildable. In the mid-1700s two men invented the Leyden jar within about a year of each other, because the same doors had opened.
